- Qualcomm recorded a $5.7 billion income-tax expense in Q4 FY2025 to establish a valuation allowance against federal deferred-tax assets. The trigger was the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted July 4, 2025. [S8]

- The law restored immediate deductions for domestic R&D beginning in FY2026 and changed preferential taxation of foreign-derived income. Qualcomm consequently expected to remain subject to the corporate alternative minimum tax (CAMT) perpetually, beginning in FY2026. CAMT imposes a 15% minimum tax on adjusted financial-statement income, reduced by general business credits. Qualcomm therefore no longer expected to realize substantially all its existing federal deferred-tax assets. [S9] [S2]

- The $5.7 billion expense was an accounting reduction in expected future tax benefits—not an equal FY2025 cash-tax payment. Qualcomm’s policy reduces deferred-tax assets to amounts more likely than not to be realized. Its cash-flow discussion explicitly says FY2025 income taxes paid were below the tax provision primarily because of this valuation-allowance charge. [S10] [S13]

- This does not mean FY2025 had no cash taxes: Qualcomm separately identified cash-tax effects from required R&D capitalization and a $530 million installment payment for the repatriation tax accrued in FY2018. [S13]

- NVIDIA FY2025, ended January 26, 2025: explicitly describes a “fabless and contracting manufacturing strategy.” TSMC and Samsung fabricate semiconductor wafers. Independent subcontractors and contract manufacturers—including Hon Hai Precision Industry, Wistron and Fabrinet—perform assembly, testing and packaging of final products. NVIDIA also identifies CoWoS packaging technology. [S1] [S9]

- NVIDIA’s model separates product development from physical manufacturing: suppliers handle all manufacturing phases and procure most raw materials, although NVIDIA directly purchases some components. NVIDIA says this avoids many costs and risks of owning manufacturing operations and lets it focus resources on design, quality assurance, marketing and customer support. [S1]

- AMD FY2025, ended December 27, 2025: identifies TSMC for wafers used in HPC, FPGA and adaptive SoC products, and GLOBALFOUNDRIES for HPC wafers at 12 nm and 14 nm. It also names TSMC, UMC and Samsung for programmable-logic ICs. Its risk disclosure specifies TSMC for all microprocessor and GPU wafers at 7 nm or smaller, with GLOBALFOUNDRIES primarily supplying larger-node wafers. [S5] [S8]

- AMD outsources board-level graphics manufacturing. Foundries sort wafers or deliver them to Asia-Pacific assembly, test, mark and packaging partners. Final semiconductor packaging and testing providers include two joint ventures with Tongfu Microelectronics, plus Siliconware Precision Industries and King Yuan Electronics. [S5]

- Comparison: both describe production models dependent on external wafer foundries and downstream assembly providers, rather than wholly internal manufacturing. NVIDIA explicitly frames this as fabless contracting and names final-product contract manufacturers; AMD describes product- and process-node-specific foundry sourcing, combined with outsourced packaging/testing and ATMP joint ventures. AMD’s joint ventures distinguish its arrangements from a description limited to independent subcontractors, but do not make its wafer fabrication internal. [S1] [S9] [S5] [S8]
